items.title: Euro futures drop to lowest level since mid-July as dollar gains.
items.excerpt: Euro futures traded lower, reaching 1.1350 before closing near 1.1365, marking the lowest level since mid-July. The decline was driven by U.S. dollar strength following rising inflation expectations and shifting Federal Reserve rate hike expectations. The euro has fallen approximately 3% since its August peak above 1.17. Meanwhile, option-derived volatility increased alongside the market decline, as measured by the CVOL index. Speculators expanded their net short positions last week, extending a continuous net short posture in euro futures since late June.

items.title: British Pound futures bounce as UK consumer confidence hits 2-year high.
items.excerpt: British Pound futures rebounded to close out the week following improved UK consumer confidence and hawkish signals from the Bank of England. After finishing higher in just two of the previous 11 sessions, the pound saw a lift as short covering emerged ahead of the weekend. Support also materialized as UK consumer confidence unexpectedly jumped to a two-year high, with GfK's index rising to minus 13 for September. Market expectations shifted as Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden and Governor Andrew Bailey highlighted inflation risks, noting that elevated energy costs could make it increasingly difficult to hold rates steady and leaving further rate hikes on the table.

items.excerpt: Key Points: Macro headwinds intensified , with surging US bond yields and a stronger dollar putting pressure on commodities, particularly precious metals. Physical tightness remains a powerful counterweight , helping industrial metals, energy and selected agricultural markets resist the broader macro pressure. Oil remains caught between improving flows and persistent disruption , as diplomacy, renewed attacks and costly workarounds keep the physical market far from normal. Copper and soybean meal highlight the supply story , with low inventories, strong demand and weather-related disruption supporting prices despite an increasingly challenging macro backdrop. items.title: Has the era of cheap food come to an end?
items.excerpt: From climate shocks, including the effects of El Niño, and rising labour costs to changing welfare standards and technological innovation, food prices may be entering a new structural regime. In this episode, Heidi Richardson and Sreedhar Mahamkali from UBS Research discuss the forces driving this shift, the potential role of technology as a counterbalance, and what a structurally higher food inflation environment could mean for consumers, businesses and markets. *(This information is subject to a disclaimer at the end of this podcast. items.title: IBIT: two ways to take part in bitcoin’s recovery without buying the shares
items.excerpt: Bitcoin has recovered roughly 37% since mid-August, and IBIT’s options market is pricing calmer conditions than the last five weeks actually delivered. Two defined-risk structures show what an investor without a position can do about that, and what each one costs. Options do not make bitcoin less volatile. They let an investor choose which slice of that volatility to take, and how much capital to put behind it. Bitcoin has risen about 37% since the middle of August, yet it remains below where it started 2026, a move backed by disclosed fund flows rather than sentiment alone: IBIT (the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF) took in roughly USD 3.76bn from 15 August (Source: Bloomberg, 22 September 2026). Investment demand remains surprisingly resilient, with Bloomberg data showing global gold ETF holdings rising by almost 50 tonnes so far in September despite the jump in real yields. items.title: Euro futures drop to 8-week lows amid hawkish Fed speak.
items.excerpt: Euro futures fell to an eight-week low of 1.1409, marking their seventh lower close in the past 10 sessions. Despite Eurozone manufacturing PMI data coming in slightly stronger than expected at 52.7, the euro continued its slide. Germany's PMI missed forecasts, dropping to 53.8, though both regions remain in expansion territory. Meanwhile, the U.S. dollar moved to multi-week highs following hawkish comments from Fed Governor Michael Barr, who signaled further rate hikes are likely needed. According to CME Group's FedWatch Tool, the probability of an October rate hike climbed to over 70%. U.S. composite PMI also reached its highest level since July 2021, reinforcing market expectations and adding further pressure to the euro as Treasury yields increased.

items.title: Global yields hit multi-year highs.
items.excerpt: Bob Iaccino of Path Trading Partners breaks down the latest market action, noting U.S. equity indices pushing lower with Nasdaq futures leading the decline. Job openings fell for the third straight month, while ISM manufacturing held in expansion territory despite missing expectations. Global yields are climbing across the board, with the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield hitting its highest level since early 2025 and the probability of a September FOMC rate hike rising. Looking ahead, focus shifts to the Fed's Beige Book, ongoing corporate earnings, and key rate decisions from the RBA and Bank of Canada.

items.title: British Pound futures slide to two-month lows on central bank divergence.
items.excerpt: British Pound futures continued their downward trajectory, trading near two-month lows after declining in six of the last seven sessions. Selling pressure persisted at 1.3330, driven by a divergence in central bank policies following the Bank of England's decision to hold rates steady while the Fed hiked. Geopolitical discussions at the United Nations also added to intraday volatility. The pullback marks a sharp reversal from a six-month high reached just four weeks ago. A similar pattern emerged in Euro futures, which also hit two-month lows as the U.S. Dollar Index climbed to a two-month high. Australian Dollar and Canadian Dollar futures experienced milder declines across a broadly softer FX complex.

items.title: Crude oil extends losses on easing supply fears.
items.excerpt: Bob Iaccino of Path Trading Partners breaks down the morning’s market action, highlighting early gains in the Russell 2000 and Nasdaq futures alongside a slight dip in the Dow. He explores the fifth consecutive session of losses for crude oil, driven by easing supply concerns in the Middle East and ongoing diplomatic efforts. The speaking schedule is also in focus, with an eye on remarks from world leaders at the UN General Assembly and multiple Federal Reserve officials. Finally, Iaccino previews the upcoming $69 billion 2-Year and $70 billion 5-Year Treasury note auctions, the latest corporate earnings, and key global PMI data.
